section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Sampling Distribution
section_1.content: Define 'sampling distribution' as the distribution of the means of many random samples taken from a population. Emphasize that we are shifting focus from individual data points to the behavior of averages.
section_1.example: Visual animation showing thousands of tiny balls being dropped into a bin; we aren't looking at one ball, but the average height of the stack.

section_2.title: The Problem: Chaos vs. Order
section_2.content: Introduce the idea that real-world populations (e.g., income, house prices) are often skewed or messy. Explain the counter-intuitive mystery: no matter how skewed the original population is, the distribution of their averages becomes predictable.
section_2.example: Visualizing a 'Skewed Monster' (a highly non-normal distribution) that somehow transforms into a perfect Bell Curve when we take the mean of multiple samples.

section_3.title: The Core Theorem: The Shape of Certainty
section_3.content: State the CLT: As sample size (n) increases, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a Normal Distribution (Bell Curve), regardless of the population's original shape. Visual focus: The 'convergence' animation where the distribution stabilizes as n goes from 5 to 30 to 100.
section_3.example: A group of robots collecting data on the weight of apples. Even if the apples are oddly shaped, the average weight of a basket of 30 apples always falls into a reliable Bell Curve.

section_4.title: Application: The Law of Large Numbers in Action
section_4.content: Explain why this matters: It allows us to perform hypothesis testing and build confidence intervals. If we know the average is normally distributed, we can predict the probability of future outcomes even without knowing the underlying population distribution.
section_4.example: A casino manager using the CLT to predict the 'average' payout of a slot machine over thousands of spins, ensuring the house always has a predictable statistical edge.

section_5.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
section_5.content: Recap: 1. Start with any shape distribution. 2. Take repeated samples. 3. Plot the means. 4. Behold the Bell Curve. The bigger the sample, the tighter the curve.
section_5.example: A final infographic showing a 'Chaos to Order' transition meter that fills up as the sample size indicator increases.
